title: Emergence of the Colonial Economy
tagline: How British rule reorganised Indian production, trade and taxation to serve the metropole, and what that did to the Indian economy.

overview.intro: Colonialism was not only a change of government; it was a reorganisation of the economy so that surplus moved from India to Britain. The East India Company began as a trading body and became a territorial and fiscal power, and by the nineteenth century the administrative, legal and transport systems of the country were being shaped to move raw material out and manufactured goods in. This unit traces that transformation: the Company’s territorial and revenue expansion, the destruction of Indian handicrafts, the land revenue systems, the growth of a colonial trade structure, and the responses of Indian industry and agriculture to it.

learn.title: From a trading company to a colonial state

blocks.text: The East India Company received its charter from the English crown in 1600 to trade in the East Indies, and for its first two centuries it was content with factories and coastal settlements. The Battle of Plassey in 1757, followed by Buxar in 1765 and the acquisition of the Diwani of Bengal, changed its character entirely. Holding the right to collect revenue meant the Company was no longer a merchant but a government, and its revenues, trade and territorial ambition became inseparable. The Regulating Act of 1773 and Pitt’s India Act of 1784 placed the Company under parliamentary supervision, while the Charter Acts progressively extended British control over Indian territory and administration.

blocks.caption: The transformation of the Company’s role
rows: Merchant with factories and a monopoly on English trade
Diwani of Bengal and the beginnings of fiscal government
Revenue systems, courts and an army ruling most of India
Direct administration under a Secretary of State

blocks.text: Once the state was in its hands, the Company reorganised revenue to guarantee a fixed and rising income. The Permanent Settlement of 1793 fixed the demand in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in perpetuity and made zamindars its revenue collectors. The Ryotwari system of southern and western India made the cultivator the direct payer to the state with a settlement that could be revised. The Mahalwari system of the north-west fixed the demand at the village or mahal level. Each system differed in who paid and how often the assessment was revised, but each had the same purpose: to secure a reliable revenue flow for the colonial treasury.

items.text: A zamindar whose estate was auctioned for arrears in the early nineteenth century.
items.note: Perpetual settlement made the demand fixed while land values changed, and default meant forfeiture.

items.text: A ryot with a settlement revised every twenty to thirty years.
items.note: The state could raise the demand after revision, so the cultivator carried the risk of change.

learn.title: The destruction of handicrafts and the reorientation of agriculture

blocks.text: Before British rule, India exported finished textiles, silk, and metal work of a quality that European manufacturers could not match. Two forces dismantled that position. The tariff policy of the nineteenth century kept duties on British cloth entering India low, while heavy duties protected the British market against Indian muslin, so the flow of manufactures reversed. Mechanisation in Lancashire then cut the price of yarn and cloth below what the handloom could achieve. The result was the ruin of weaving and spinning communities, who were driven back onto the land for survival, which in turn increased pressure on agriculture and lowered the cultivator’s income.

blocks.caption: Causes and consequences of the decline of Indian handicrafts
rows: Indian textiles priced out of the British market while British cloth entered India cheaply
Machine yarn and cloth undercut hand-spun and hand-woven goods
Court demand for luxury craft goods collapsed under colonial rule
Cheaper transport favoured mill goods over local craft production
Capital that might have modernised industry left the country

blocks.text: Agriculture was reoriented toward cash crops to serve colonial industry and trade. Indigo was forced on cultivators in Bengal and Bihar, opium was grown for export to China, and later cotton, jute, tea and coffee expanded on plantations. Food crop area was squeezed, so famines became more frequent and more severe when rains failed, and the cultivator often had to sell at low prices to meet a revenue demand that did not vary with the harvest.

items: Cash crops replaced food crops, reducing the cultivator’s own food security.
Revenue was demanded in cash, forcing sale of produce even in a poor year.
Moneylenders advanced credit and often took land in default.
Land ceased to be a source of status and became a commodity that could be transferred.
Famines of the nineteenth century were sharpened by the reorientation of agriculture.

learn.title: The drain of wealth and the colonial trade structure

blocks.text: Dadabhai Naoroji articulated the drain theory in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, arguing that a portion of India’s income was transferred to Britain every year through the home charges of the colonial government, the savings of British officials, and the profits of British enterprise, without any corresponding goods or services in return. Even a small annual percentage, compounded over decades, represented a substantial subtraction from the country’s capacity to save and invest. R.C. Dutt developed the argument with revenue and trade statistics, and the theory became a central plank of nationalist economic criticism.

blocks.caption: The structure of colonial trade
rows: Raw cotton, jute, indigo, opium, tea, hides
Cash crops expanded at the cost of food crops
Native industry priced out of its own market
Home charges, salaries, freight and insurance
A steady outflow with no goods in return
Owned abroad, with profits remitted abroad

items.text: Home charges covering the Secretary of State’s office in London.
items.note: An administrative cost of the colony borne by Indian revenue and not repaid in goods.

items.text: Cotton shipped to Lancashire and returned as cloth.
items.note: The value addition happened in Britain, so India earned raw material prices for finished goods.

learn.title: Infrastructure, responses and the colonial legacy

blocks.text: The colonial economy did build infrastructure: a railway network from 1853, the telegraph, canals, and a unified postal system and currency. These served military and administrative control and the movement of raw material to ports as much as they served Indian needs, but they also knit the internal market together and made large-scale migration and news possible. Indian responses took several forms: swadeshi advocacy of home-made goods, the founding of joint-stock mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, the articulation of economic critique by Naoroji, Dadabhai and Ranade, and the formation of chambers of commerce pressing for tariff protection.

blocks.caption: Assessment of colonial infrastructure
rows: Military movement and raw material to ports
Connected the internal market and lowered transport cost
Export of raw material, import of manufactures
Provided finance, largely for colonial trade

items: Joint-stock textile mills from the 1850s were the first major Indian industrial response.
The swadeshi movement of 1905 made the boycott of foreign cloth a mass political act.
Economic nationalists used data to argue the case for self-government.
The colonial legacy was an economy oriented outward, with a narrow industrial base and high rural distress.

questions.prompt: The Battle of Plassey in 1757 is significant because it:
options: Ended the East India Company’s trade
Began the Company’s territorial power in India
questions.answer: Began the Company’s territorial power in India
questions.explanation: Plassey gave the Company influence over Bengal and, with the Diwani in 1765, made it a revenue-collecting territorial power.

questions.prompt: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 was introduced in:
questions.explanation: Cornwallis’s settlement applied to Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and fixed the revenue demand with zamindars in perpetuity.

questions.prompt: The chief cause of the decline of Indian handicrafts in the nineteenth century was:
options: Tariff policy favouring British manufactures together with mechanisation
questions.answer: Tariff policy favouring British manufactures together with mechanisation
questions.explanation: Duties kept Indian cloth out of Britain while British cloth entered India cheaply, and Lancashire machinery undercut handloom prices.

questions.prompt: The drain of wealth theory was formulated most fully by:
questions.explanation: Naoroji set out the argument in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, and R.C. Dutt supported it with revenue data.

questions.prompt: The system in which the cultivator paid revenue directly to the state is known as the __________ system.
questions.explanation: The Ryotwari settlement applied mainly in southern and western India and allowed the demand to be revised at intervals.

questions.prompt: The forced cultivation of __________ in Bengal and Bihar was one of the most resented features of colonial agriculture.
questions.explanation: Indigo was grown for European dye works under contracts that left the cultivator little choice and poor returns.

questions.prompt: State four causes of the decline of Indian handicrafts.
questions.answer: Four causes are: tariff policy that protected the British market against Indian textiles while admitting British cloth into India cheaply; mechanisation of Lancashire mills, which produced yarn and cloth below handloom cost; the loss of princely patronage as courts were dissolved or reduced under colonial rule; and the expansion of railways, which carried cheap mill goods into the interior. The drain of capital is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each cause needs the mechanism stated, since a bare list earns only partial marks.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Ryotwari and the Mahalwari systems of land revenue.
questions.answer: In the Ryotwari system the cultivator, or ryot, was assessed and paid the revenue directly to the state, with the settlement open to revision at intervals, and it applied mainly in southern and western India. In the Mahalwari system the village or mahal as a whole was made responsible for the payment, with the demand fixed for the community and collectors appointed for it, and it applied in the north-western and central regions. The Permanent Settlement differed from both because zamindars paid and the demand was fixed permanently.
questions.explanation: Three systems must be distinguished by who paid and whether the demand was revisable.

questions.prompt: Explain the drain of wealth theory and assess its significance for Indian nationalism.
questions.answer: The drain theory holds that a portion of India’s income was transferred to Britain each year without any corresponding return of goods or services. Dadabhai Naoroji set it out most fully in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, and the channels were the home charges of the colonial government including the India Office in London, the savings remitted by British officials, and the profits of British-owned enterprises, freight and insurance paid to British firms. R.C. Dutt supported the argument with revenue and trade figures showing India’s exports exceeding imports in value while the difference was settled in payments rather than in goods. Its significance for nationalism was that it converted a general sense of hardship into a measurable accusation: if wealth left annually, poverty was not a natural condition but a consequence of rule, and reforming or ending that rule became an economic as well as a political demand. The theory shaped the nationalist case for swadeshi, for tariff protection and eventually for self-government.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the channels of transfer, the evidence offered and the political consequence of the argument.

questions.prompt: Railways are often described as the most beneficial colonial investment. Evaluate this claim using evidence of their purpose and their effects.
questions.answer: The claim has to be tested on both sides. In favour: from the first line in 1853 the railways cut the cost and time of moving goods and people across a vast country, knit regional markets into a national one, carried grain to famine areas, enabled migration and the spread of news, and later supported Indian-owned industry by moving coal and cotton. Against: the capital was raised in Britain on guaranteed returns, so the risk was borne by Indian revenue while the profits went abroad; the route planning favoured the movement of raw material to the ports and of troops, not the connection of Indian producers to Indian consumers; the rolling stock and much of the finance were British, so the railways did not build an Indian engineering base; and the guarantee itself was a drain on the treasury. A balanced judgement is that the railways were beneficial in their eventual effects but were designed as an instrument of control and of export, and their financing transferred value outward. The infrastructure therefore served colonial purposes first and Indian development incidentally, which is the pattern of the colonial economy as a whole.
questions.explanation: Marks are for holding both sides with specific evidence and reaching a judgement about purpose versus effect rather than simply listing advantages.
